newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS- S-E BANKEN DISAPPOINTS AS H1 COSTS RISE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- S-E BANKEN DISAPPOINTS AS H1 COSTS RISE.

text.p: S-E-Banken, the first of Sweden's big four to report, disappointed the market on Tuesday by announcing a lower than expected six-month profit with rising costs.
The bank posted an operating profit of 2.86 billion crowns ($356.8 million) which was lower than market expectations of 3.02 billion crowns.
But lower credit losses lifted the operating profit seven percent from the first half of 1996.

"This improvement is primarily due to declining lending losses. Total income is growing in spite of the contiued pressure on margins," said Jacob Wallenberg, president and group chief executive, in a statement.

The bank said lending losses plummeted by 70 percent to 250 million crowns and the lending loss level dropped to 0.18 percent from 0.67 percent a year earlier. Doubtful claims fell 20 percent to 4.81 billion crowns.
But costs rose 12 percent to 4.86 billion crowns, with more than half stemming from expanding staff numbers and the rest from data development and marketing.

"More than half of the increase is attributable to aggressive investment decisions, which are indispensible for the bank's increased focus on information technology (IT), asset management and an expanded presence in the Nordic countries," Wallenberg said.

S-E-Banken said deposits from the general public rose 14 percent from a year ago and the bank increased its market share to 19.1 percent from 17.8 percent mostly because of higher deposits from companies and municipalities in Swedish crowns and foreign currencies.
"In Sweden and in many other countries private savings are on the swing," Wallenberg said.
"Total private savings in S-E-Banken increased by 21 percent compared with the same period last year and our market share has thus grown from 16.5 percent to 17.1 percent.
"Mutual funds capture an increasing share of savings at the expense of traditional deposits. We believe this trend will continue."

Net interest earnings increased 24 percent to 4.28 billion crowns, mainly lifted by rising interest income from the bank's portfolios as the gap between long and short term interest rates was wider than in the first half of 1996. But net interest earnings were negatively affected by the continued decline in margins, the bank said.
The bank's share of equities trading rose to 11.6 percent in the first six months of the year from 9.9 percent.
Shares in the bank, whose full name is Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, traded four crowns lower at 94.5 after the result compared to a range of 98 and 98.5 ahead of the report.
